name: Voice of the Customer (LLM)
description: Mine 200 raw product reviews with Bedrock LLMs — sentiment, issue themes, structured extraction, and semantic search — then join the signals back to Athena revenue to build a product action plan. Shows invoke_llm, llm_sentiment, llm_classify, llm_extract, embed_texts, semantic_search, llm_summarize and count_tokens tied to real DynamoDB + Athena + S3 data.

cells.code:
# 🗣️ Voice of the Customer

**The problem:** Athena tells us *what* sells and *how much*. It cannot tell us **why** customers are unhappy — that story is locked in **free-text reviews** no SQL `GROUP BY` can read. So a product can be a **top seller with a quietly rising churn risk**, and the dashboards never show it.

This workbook mines the raw review text with **Amazon Bedrock LLMs** (via the pre-loaded `llm_*` helpers — no API keys, the MicroVM's execution role does the auth), turns it into **structured signals**, and joins those back to the revenue data to produce a **product action plan a merchandising manager can act on today**.

| Step | Question | Source | Helper |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | Which products drive the money? | `orders` × `products` (**Athena**) | SQL |
| Raw voice | What are customers actually saying? | `ecommerce-reviews` (**DynamoDB**) | `read_dynamodb` |
| Sentiment | Is each review positive or negative? | review text | `llm_sentiment` |
| Themes | What KIND of problem is it? | review text | `llm_classify` |
| Structure | Pull issue + aspect + recommend flag | review text | `llm_extract` |
| Search | Find a specific complaint, no keywords | review text | `embed_texts` + `semantic_search` |
| Brief | Summarize the worst product's reviews | review text | `llm_summarize` |

```mermaid
graph LR
  A["Athena: orders × products"] --> J["Revenue × Voice join"]
  D["DynamoDB: review text"] --> S["llm_sentiment"]
  D --> C["llm_classify: issue theme"]
  D --> E["llm_extract: aspect + recommend"]

```

**Run all cells top-to-bottom.** Every LLM call is metered per token — this notebook works on the 200-row sample; `count_tokens` (Step 2) shows the size before the big calls.

## Step 0 · Connect to the sandbox

Confirm identity and resolve the artifacts bucket. Everything runs inside the MicroVM using its **execution role** — the same role authorizes Athena, DynamoDB, and Bedrock, so there are no credentials in the notebook.

import pandas as pd
info = whoami()
account, region = info['account'], info['region']
bucket = info['bucket']
print(f"\nReady on account {account} · {region}")

## Step 1 · The money — top products by revenue (Athena)

One SQL query joins **Athena** `orders` × `products` to rank products by revenue and margin. This is the *structured* half of the picture — the half every dashboard already shows. Saved as `product_revenue`.

-- Athena: revenue, units, and margin per product
SELECT
  p.product_id,
  p.name,
  p.category,
  p.brand,
  ROUND((p.price - p.cost) / p.price * 100, 1) AS margin_pct,
  COUNT(o.order_id)                            AS order_count,
  SUM(o.quantity)                              AS units_sold,
  ROUND(SUM(o.total), 2)                       AS revenue
FROM microvm_demo_db.orders o
JOIN microvm_demo_db.products p ON o.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY p.product_id, p.name, p.category, p.brand, p.price, p.cost
ORDER BY revenue DESC

## Step 2 · The voice — raw review text (DynamoDB)

The *why* lives in **DynamoDB** `ecommerce-reviews`: one row per review with a 1–5 `rating`, a `title`, and free-text `text`. We pull them all into a DataFrame, join each review to its product name/category from Step 1 (so themes are grounded in a real product), and use **`count_tokens`** to size the review corpus **before** we spend any LLM calls on it.

# @param {"type": "slider", "min": 20, "max": 200, "step": 10, "default": 80, "label": "Reviews to analyze"}
max_reviews = 80

# Pull the raw reviews from DynamoDB (full scan of the 200-row sample table)
reviews = read_dynamodb('ecommerce-reviews')
reviews = reviews.rename(columns={'productId': 'product_id'})
reviews['rating'] = pd.to_numeric(reviews['rating'], errors='coerce')

# Attach product name/category from the Athena result so signals are grounded
prod_lookup = product_revenue[['product_id', 'name', 'category']]
reviews = reviews.merge(prod_lookup, on='product_id', how='left')

# The llm_* helpers run one Bedrock call per row (CONCURRENTLY, so ~80 rows finish
# in a few seconds). We still cap the sample so a demo cell stays snappy and cheap —
# drag the slider up to analyze more, or remove the cap for the full table.
reviews = reviews.head(max_reviews).reset_index(drop=True)

print(f"{len(reviews)} reviews across {reviews['product_id'].nunique()} products")
# Size the text corpus BEFORE the LLM passes — tokens drive cost + latency
total_tokens = count_tokens(reviews['text'].tolist())
print(f"~{total_tokens:,} tokens of review text to process")
reviews[['product_id', 'name', 'rating', 'title', 'text']].head()

## Step 3 · Sentiment every review can't lie about — `llm_sentiment`

The star rating is a blunt instrument (plenty of 3-star reviews are scathing in the text, and some 4-star reviews flag a real defect). **`llm_sentiment`** reads the actual prose and labels each review **negative / neutral / positive** — something no SQL aggregate can do. We then compare the LLM's read to the star rating to find **rating/text mismatches** (the reviews that need a human).

# LLM sentiment over the review TEXT (one Bedrock call per review, with backoff)
sent = llm_sentiment(reviews['text'])
reviews['sentiment'] = sent['sentiment'].values

print('Sentiment mix (from the text, not the stars):')
print(reviews['sentiment'].value_counts().to_string())

# Where the text disagrees with the star rating — the reviews worth reading
mismatch = reviews[((reviews['rating'] >= 4) & (reviews['sentiment'] == 'negative')) |
                   ((reviews['rating'] <= 2) & (reviews['sentiment'] == 'positive'))]
print(f"\n{len(mismatch)} rating/text MISMATCHES (high stars but negative text, or vice-versa)")
mismatch[['product_id', 'name', 'rating', 'sentiment', 'text']].head(8)

## Step 4 · What KIND of problem? — `llm_classify`

Knowing a review is negative isn't actionable; knowing it's a **sizing** problem vs a **shipping** problem is. **`llm_classify`** buckets each review into a fixed set of issue themes. We only classify the **negative** reviews (that's where the action is), which also keeps the token spend down.

ISSUE_LABELS = ['quality', 'sizing/fit', 'shipping/packaging', 'value/price', 'usability', 'customer service', 'other']

neg = reviews[reviews['sentiment'] == 'negative'].copy()
if len(neg):
    themed = llm_classify(
        neg['text'],
        labels=ISSUE_LABELS,
        instructions="Pick the single dominant complaint. If it's about defects or breakage, use 'quality'.",
    )
    neg['issue'] = themed['label'].values
    print('Complaint themes across negative reviews:')
    print(neg['issue'].value_counts().to_string())
else:
    print('No negative reviews to classify at this sample.')
neg[['name', 'rating', 'issue', 'text']].head(8)

## Step 5 · Turn prose into columns — `llm_extract`

For a tidy, joinable table we need **structure**, not paragraphs. **`llm_extract`** pulls a fixed schema out of each negative review — the specific product **aspect**, a one-line **issue summary**, and a **would_recommend** flag — so free text becomes columns you can pivot, filter, and join like any other DataFrame.

## Step 6 · The danger zone — join voice back to revenue

Now the payoff: fuse the **LLM voice signals** with the **Athena revenue** from Step 1. A product that sells a lot **and** carries a high negative-sentiment share is the one bleeding future revenue while today's dashboard still looks green. Saved as `product_voice`.

# Per-product voice metrics from the LLM signals
voice = reviews.groupby('product_id').agg(
    reviews=('sentiment', 'size'),
    negative=('sentiment', lambda s: (s == 'negative').sum()),
    avg_rating=('rating', 'mean'),
).reset_index()
voice['negative_pct'] = (voice['negative'] / voice['reviews'] * 100).round(1)

# Fuse with Athena revenue → one row per product, money + mood together
product_voice = product_revenue.merge(voice, on='product_id', how='left')
product_voice['negative_pct'] = product_voice['negative_pct'].fillna(0)
product_voice['reviews'] = product_voice['reviews'].fillna(0).astype(int)

# Danger zone: top-half revenue AND above-average negativity
rev_median = product_voice['revenue'].median()
neg_bar = product_voice.loc[product_voice['reviews'] > 0, 'negative_pct'].mean()
danger = product_voice[(product_voice['revenue'] >= rev_median) &
                       (product_voice['negative_pct'] > neg_bar)].sort_values('revenue', ascending=False)
print(f"{len(danger)} high-revenue products with above-average negative sentiment (>{neg_bar:.0f}%):")
danger[['name', 'category', 'revenue', 'reviews', 'negative_pct', 'avg_rating']].head(10)

# Portfolio map: revenue vs negativity. Top-right = sells well AND complained about.
plot_scatter(product_voice[product_voice['reviews'] > 0],
             x='negative_pct', y='revenue', size='reviews', color='category',
             title='Revenue vs negative-sentiment share (bubble = # reviews)')

## Step 7 · Ask the reviews a question — semantic search

Keyword search misses paraphrases ("died after a week" never contains the word *battery*). **`embed_texts`** turns every review into a vector once, and **`semantic_search`** finds the closest reviews to a natural-language query — reusing the cached vectors so only the query is embedded on each search.

⚙️ *Slider:* how many matches to return.

# Embed the review corpus ONCE, then reuse the vectors for any number of searches
corpus = reviews['text'].tolist()
review_vecs = embed_texts(corpus)
print(f"Embedded {review_vecs.shape[0]} reviews into {review_vecs.shape[1]}-dim vectors")

# @param {"type": "slider", "min": 3, "max": 15, "step": 1, "default": 5, "label": "Matches to return"}
top_k = 5
# @param {"type": "dropdown", "options": ["stopped working after a short time", "cheaper than it looks / feels flimsy", "wrong size or poor fit", "arrived damaged in the box", "great value, exceeded expectations"], "default": "stopped working after a short time", "label": "Search the reviews for..."}
query = "stopped working after a short time"

# Only the query is embedded here — corpus vectors are reused (fast + cheap)
hits = semantic_search(query, corpus, corpus_vectors=review_vecs, top_k=top_k)
# Attach the product name for context
hits = hits.merge(reviews[['text', 'name', 'rating']].drop_duplicates('text'),
                  on='text', how='left')
print(f"Closest reviews to: \"{query}\"")
hits[['score', 'name', 'rating', 'text']]

## Step 8 · The brief — summarize the worst product's reviews

Finally, take the single highest-revenue product in the danger zone and hand a manager a **decision-ready brief**: **`llm_summarize`** condenses all of its negative reviews into a few bullet points, and **`invoke_llm`** turns that into one recommended action. This is the last mile — from 200 raw reviews to a sentence someone acts on.

if len(danger):
    target = danger.iloc[0]
    target_reviews = reviews[(reviews['product_id'] == target['product_id']) &
                             (reviews['sentiment'] == 'negative')]['text'].tolist()
    print(f"Target: {target['name']}  (${target['revenue']:,.0f} revenue · {target['negative_pct']:.0f}% negative)")
    print(f"Summarizing {len(target_reviews)} negative reviews...\n")

    # Summarize the complaints into bullets
    brief = llm_summarize('\n\n'.join(target_reviews), style='bullets', max_words=90)
    print('WHAT CUSTOMERS ARE SAYING:')
    print(brief)

    # Turn the brief into a single recommended action
    action = invoke_llm(
        f"A top-selling product has these recurring complaints:\n{brief}\n\n"
        f"In ONE sentence, recommend the single highest-impact action for the merchandising team.",
        system="You are a pragmatic retail merchandising advisor. Be specific and concise.",
    )
    print('\nRECOMMENDED ACTION:')
    print(action)
else:
    print('No danger-zone product at this sample — try re-running; the review sample varies.')

## Step 9 · Ship it to regional teams — `llm_translate`

The brief and the recommended action are in English, but the merchandising teams that act on them are global. **`llm_translate`** localizes the action into the languages your regional owners read — a string → a string, or a whole column → a DataFrame(`text`, `translation`). Target language is required; the source is auto-detected.

⚙️ *Slider:* which markets to localize for.

# @param {"type": "dropdown", "options": ["French,Spanish,Japanese", "French,German", "Spanish,Portuguese", "Japanese,Korean"], "default": "French,Spanish,Japanese", "label": "Localize for markets"}
markets = "French,Spanish,Japanese"
langs = [m.strip() for m in markets.split(',') if m.strip()]

if 'action' in dir() and action:
    # One target language → a string.
    print(f"EN: {action}\n")
    for lang in langs:
        print(f"{lang}: {llm_translate(action, to=lang)}\n")

    # A whole LIST of languages at once → a tidy DataFrame(text, translation).
    localized = llm_translate([action] * len(langs), to=langs[0]) if False else None
    # (Per-language above is clearer here; llm_translate on a list translates every
    #  item into ONE target — use it when you have many SOURCE texts, one target.)
else:
    print('Run Step 8 first so there is a recommended `action` to translate.')

## Recap

We went from **structured revenue** (Athena) + **unstructured reviews** (DynamoDB) to an **action** — using LLMs for exactly the part SQL can't do: reading text at scale.

- **`llm_sentiment`** graded the prose and exposed rating/text mismatches.
- **`llm_classify`** bucketed complaints into themes; **`llm_extract`** turned prose into joinable columns.
- The **join back to revenue** surfaced high-revenue products with a rising negativity problem — the danger zone.
- **`embed_texts` + `semantic_search`** answered plain-language questions over the reviews with no keywords.
- **`llm_summarize` + `invoke_llm`** produced a manager-ready brief and a single recommended action.
- **`llm_translate`** localized that action for regional teams.

Every LLM call ran on Amazon Bedrock through the MicroVM's execution role — no keys in the notebook. Swap the model with the `model=` argument on any `llm_*` helper (see `list_bedrock_models()` for what's available), and point the same pattern at **your** review, ticket, or feedback text.
